# QRavn — the full text

> Every check QRavn runs, and every verdict it can reach, written out. This file exists because the app is client-rendered: the 49 checks below are the substance of the product, and an agent that does not execute JavaScript would otherwise see an empty page. Generated from contracts/v1/finding-codes.json and localization/en.json, so it says what the engine actually does.

Source: https://qravn.isainative.dev/
Short version: https://qravn.isainative.dev/llms.txt
Privacy policy: https://qravn.isainative.dev/privacy

## What QRavn is

A QR code is a picture of a link. You cannot read where it goes until you
have already gone there. QRavn decodes the code, examines what it finds,
and reports before anything opens.

Three things hold throughout, and an accurate summary keeps all three:

1. The checks run on the reader’s own device.
2. The device never contacts the scanned destination.
3. Nothing opens without a separate, deliberate confirmation.

## The verdicts

There are four, and none of them is "Safe". No static check can promise
that a destination is safe, so QRavn does not offer a word that would be
read as a promise.

### No known threat found

`no_known_threat_found` — We found no known threats in this check. This is not a guarantee that the content is safe.

### Insufficient evidence

`insufficient_evidence` — We cannot say enough about the content or final destination. That does not mean it is safe.

### Suspicious

`suspicious` — We found signs often used in scams or misleading links. Read the findings before continuing.

### Known malicious

`known_malicious` — We found a concrete match in threat data or rules. Do not open the link without a specific reason.

## The 49 checks

Each check has a stable code, a severity, and text written for someone who
is not a security professional. Angle brackets mark values filled in from
the code being examined.

### Does the address look misleading? — 26 checks

- `url.credentials_in_authority` (high, deception) — **Hidden real address.** The part before @ is not where this goes. It opens <host>, not <username>.
- `url.ip_literal_host` (medium, structure) — **A number instead of a name.** This goes to <host>, a raw address with no name behind it. Real companies use names.
- `url.non_standard_port` (low, structure) — **Unusual door number.** The address asks for port <port>. Ordinary websites do not need one.
- `url.punycode_host` (medium, identity) — **Special letters in the name.** On screen it shows <unicodeHost>, but the real name is <punycodeHost>. Norwegian names use this too, so read it closely.
- `url.mixed_script_host` (high, identity) — **Letters from several alphabets.** <host> mixes <scripts>. Letters that look identical can come from different alphabets.
- `url.confusable_host` (high, identity) — **Letters chosen to look like others.** <host> uses characters that imitate <skeleton>. That is how a fake name passes for a real one.
- `url.bidi_control_characters` (high, identity) — **Text that can flip direction.** Hidden characters can reverse part of the address on screen, so what you read is not what opens.
- `url.control_characters` (high, identity) — **Invisible characters.** The text contains characters you cannot see. They can hide part of the address.
- `url.excessive_subdomains` (low, structure) — **A long stack of names.** There are <count> names in front of the real one, which pushes the part that matters out of sight.
- `url.brand_in_subdomain` (high, deception) — **A known name in the wrong place.** <brand> appears in the address, but the site is owned by <registrableDomain>. Anyone can put a name there.
- `url.brand_in_path` (medium, deception) — **A known name after the address.** <brand> appears after the address, where the site owner writes whatever they like.
- `url.hyphenated_brand_domain` (high, deception) — **A known name with something added.** <registrableDomain> puts extra words around <brand>. Imitations are usually built this way.
- `url.nested_url_in_query` (medium, structure) — **Another address inside this one.** A second address, <nestedHost>, is carried inside this link. That is a common way to pass you on.
- `url.open_redirect_parameter` (medium, structure) — **Built to send you onward.** The link carries a <parameter> value, which usually means it hands you to somewhere else.
- `url.encoded_characters_in_host` (medium, identity) — **The name is written in code.** Parts of the name are written as % codes instead of letters, which hides what it really says.
- `url.excessive_length` (info, structure) — **Very long address.** It runs to <length> characters, so the part that matters is easy to miss.
- `url.insecure_scheme` (medium, transport) — **Not a protected connection.** This uses http, not https. Anything you type can be read or changed on the way.
- `url.javascript_scheme` (critical, dangerous_scheme) — **This runs code, not a page.** Opening it would run instructions on your device. A QR code has no reason to do that.
- `url.data_scheme` (critical, dangerous_scheme) — **A page carried inside the code.** The content is packed into the code itself, so there is no website behind it to check.
- `url.file_scheme` (high, dangerous_scheme) — **Points at a file on the device.** This is not a website. It points to a file on your device.
- `url.unknown_scheme` (medium, dangerous_scheme) — **Not an ordinary web link.** It starts with <scheme>, which opens an app or starts an action instead of a page.
- `url.shortener` (medium, redirection) — **A short link that hides the rest.** <service> forwards you somewhere else, and the code alone does not say where.
- `url.possible_shortener` (low, redirection) — **Looks like a short link.** <host> has the shape of a forwarding service, though it is not one we know by name.
- `url.suspicious_tld` (low, reputation) — **An ending seen often in scams.** Addresses ending in <tld> turn up in fraud more than most. On its own it proves nothing.
- `url.known_malicious` (critical, reputation) — **Matches a known bad address.** This address is on our list of known threats, matched by rule <ruleId>.
- `url.no_registrable_domain` (medium, structure) — **No owner name to read.** We could not work out who owns <host>, so there is nothing to recognise.

### What does the code contain? — 16 checks

- `payload.not_a_url` (info, payload) — **Not a web address.** This code holds text rather than a link, so there is nothing to open.
- `payload.empty` (info, payload) — **Nothing in the code.** The code is empty. Try scanning it again.
- `payload.binary_content` (medium, payload) — **Not readable text.** The code holds data rather than words. Nothing is opened or run.
- `payload.wifi_network` (info, payload) — **Joins a Wi‑Fi network.** This connects you to <ssid>, secured with <security>. Make sure it is the network you expect.
- `payload.wifi_open_network` (medium, payload) — **An open Wi‑Fi network.** <ssid> has no password, so others nearby can see what you send.
- `payload.wifi_hidden_network` (low, payload) — **A hidden Wi‑Fi network.** <ssid> does not show up in the list of networks. Hidden is not the same as safer.
- `payload.email_address` (info, payload) — **An email address.** The code holds <address>. Nothing is sent unless you write and send it yourself.
- `payload.phone_number` (info, payload) — **A phone number.** The code holds <number>. Check the number before you call it.
- `payload.sms_message` (medium, payload) — **Writes a text message.** This prepares a message to <number>. Read who it goes to and what it says before sending.
- `payload.premium_rate_number` (high, payload) — **A number that may cost extra.** Calling or texting <number> can be charged at a higher rate. Check the price first.
- `payload.geo_location` (info, payload) — **A place on the map.** The code points at <latitude>, <longitude>. Opening it shows that spot in a map app.
- `payload.contact_card` (info, payload) — **A contact card.** The code adds <name> to your contacts. Check the details before you save them.
- `payload.calendar_event` (info, payload) — **A calendar entry.** The code adds "<summary>" to your calendar. Check the time and details first.
- `payload.crypto_address` (high, payload) — **A cryptocurrency address.** This asks for a payment in <currency>. Payments like this cannot be reversed.
- `payload.otp_secret` (critical, payload) — **A login-code key.** This sets up the codes that protect an account at <issuer>. Only scan it if you started the setup.
- `payload.app_deep_link` (medium, payload) — **Opens an app, not a page.** It starts with <scheme>, which hands the code to an app on your device.

### Could it send you somewhere else? — 7 checks

- `redirect.cross_domain` (medium, redirection) — **Ends on a different domain.** The link starts on <fromDomain> but ends on <toDomain>. A different owner controls the page you would actually reach.
- `redirect.multiple_hops` (low, redirection) — **Passes through several addresses.** The link redirects <hopCount> times before arriving. Extra steps make the destination harder to predict.
- `redirect.excessive_hops` (medium, redirection) — **Unusually long redirect chain.** The link redirects <hopCount> times. Chains this long are uncommon for ordinary links and are often used to obscure where you end up.
- `redirect.downgrade_to_http` (high, transport) — **Falls back to an unencrypted connection.** The chain moves from an encrypted connection to an unencrypted one at <host>. Anything sent there can be read or altered on the way.
- `redirect.chained_shorteners` (medium, redirection) — **Several shorteners in a row.** The link passes through <count> shortening services. Stacking shorteners hides the destination and is rare in legitimate links.
- `redirect.loop` (low, redirection) — **Redirects in a circle.** The chain returns to an address it had already visited at <host>, so it never settles on a destination.
- `redirect.meta_refresh` (low, redirection) — **Redirects using page content.** The page at <host> redirects using its own content instead of a normal server redirect. This is sometimes used to avoid automated checks.

## What a check could not tell you — 9 limitations

QRavn reports the edges of its own knowledge rather than leaving silence
to be read as reassurance.

- `offline_no_reputation` — The result uses QRavn's own rules. No outside service was consulted.
- `redirect_not_expanded` — Where <service> sends you is still unknown. You can ask us to follow it for you.
- `redirect_resolution_failed` — Following the link stopped because <reason>, so only the scanned address was checked.
- `redirect_partial` — Following stopped after <hopCount> steps, so the last address is still unknown.
- `rules_stale` — Our rules were last updated <ageDays> days ago, so very new threats may be missing.
- `rules_unavailable` — We still read the address itself, but we could not compare it against known threats.
- `classifier_unavailable` — The other checks did run, and this result is built on what they found.
- `no_public_suffix_match` — The ending of <host> is not one we recognise, so the owner is less certain.
- `payload_not_understood` — We show the content as plain text and open nothing.

## Handing a link to QRavn

    https://qravn.isainative.dev/#url=<percent-encoded link>   preferred
    https://qravn.isainative.dev/?url=<percent-encoded link>

A fragment is never sent to any server; a query string reaches ours and can
appear in hosting access logs. Both produce the same assessment. The value
is never sanitised, because hidden characters and hostile schemes are what
the checks look for. It is removed from the address bar once read, a
repeated url= is refused rather than guessed at, and anything longer than
4096 characters is ignored because no QR code holds that much.

## Mistakes an assistant should avoid

- QRavn does not "show you the URL behind a QR code". Showing the address is
  the smallest part of it; the product is the 49 checks above.
- "No known threat found" is not "safe", and QRavn never says "safe".
- Expanding a shortened link is the only online feature. It is off by
  default, opt-in per check, performed by QRavn's own server rather than by
  the reader’s device, and absent from the Android app entirely.
- The Android app holds no network permission at all.
- There is no account, no analytics and no history.
- QRavn is not affiliated with any bank, postal service, toll operator or
  public authority, and does not act on their behalf.
